seeds.ex: Raise a specific exception. Catch the one you can handle. A SyntaxError means the file is not valid Python. A TypeError means an operation does not apply to that type. A ValueError means the type is right and the value is not. KeyError and IndexError are lookup failures.
seeds.eg: def parse_age(text): try: age = int(text) except ValueError as exc: raise ValueError("age must be an integer") from exc if age < 0: raise ValueError("age must be >= 0") return age

seeds.ex: A test is a program that fails when the behavior changes. An environment keeps its installs separate. unittest ships with Python. A test method starts with test_, and assertions such as assertEqual fail the test. pytest is a widely used third-party runner with a lighter style. It is not the standard library.
seeds.eg: import unittest class TestGreet(unittest.TestCase): def test_comma(self): self.assertEqual(greet("Ada"), "Hello, Ada")

seeds.ex: A list is a mutable sequence. A tuple is an immutable one. append adds at the end and, in CPython, is amortized constant time. Inserting at the front shifts every later item, so it grows with the length. A slice copies. Sorting a list with sort changes it. sorted returns a new list. A tuple can be a dict key when its items are hashable.

A dict maps a hashable key to a value and remembers insertion order. In CPython, lookup, insert, and delete for dict and set are constant time on average. Hash collisions and resizing mean a single operation can cost more. Say "average case in CPython" when you quote that. set stores unique hashable items. Use it for membership tests.
seeds.eg: def counts(words): found = {} for word in words: found[word] = found.get(word, 0) + 1 return found

seeds.ex: A list can be a stack. A deque is the honest queue. heapq is a priority queue. append and pop on a list are a stack. A queue wants cheap removal from the other end, which is collections.deque and popleft. Indexing the middle of a deque is not the cheap operation. heapq keeps the smallest item at index 0 of a list, with heappush and heappop.

A tree is a node and its children. A graph is nodes and edges, and it may contain cycles. A nested dict or a small class is enough for a tree. A graph is often a dict from a node to its neighbors. Depth-first search uses a stack, or recursion. Breadth-first search uses a queue.

sorted is the tool. Binary search is the idea, and bisect is the module. CPython's sorted is a stable Timsort. It accepts a key function. Binary search only works on sorted data and halves the remaining range each time. The bisect module does that for you. Knowing the idea matters in an interview. Replacing bisect in a program rarely does.

Name the structure, the operation, and whether you mean average or worst case. Say "list append is amortized constant time in CPython" rather than "lists are O(1)". Say which operation. Lookup in a dict is not the same cost as "the dict". The TimeComplexity wiki is a useful CPython note.

Walk a sequence with two indices instead of nested loops when the order or window size lets you. Checking every pair in a sequence of length n with two nested loops visits n * (n - 1) // 2 pairs (quadratic growth).
Break a problem into smaller subproblems and cache repeated calls with functools.cache. A recursive function needs a base case that stops and a step that moves toward the base case.

Use it when the program spends time waiting, not when it spends time calculating. A download, a database call, or a timer leaves the CPU idle. await marks a place where this coroutine can pause so another one can run. A tight numerical loop does not pause, so marking it async does not make it faster.

Calling an async function returns a coroutine. A task schedules it. async def defines a coroutine function. Calling it does not run the body. It returns a coroutine. asyncio.create_task schedules that coroutine. await waits for a result and gives the loop a chance to run something else. asyncio.gather runs several awaitables and collects their results.
seeds.eg: import asyncio async def delayed_sum(a, b): await asyncio.sleep(0) return a + b

seeds.ex: A task you never await can fail in silence. A timeout should be a choice. If you create a task and drop the only reference, you can miss its exception. Await it, or keep the task and attach a done callback you actually read. asyncio.timeout, or wait_for, puts a bound on how long you are willing to wait.

The interpreter stores annotations. A type checker reads them. Since Python 3.14, annotations are evaluated lazily, as specified by PEP 649 and PEP 749. You can refer to a class that is defined later without quoting the name. The annotationlib module inspects them. None of that adds a check at call time.
seeds.eg: def greet(name: str) -> str: return f"Hello, {name}"

seeds.ex: list[int], unions, TypedDict, and Protocol cover most everyday hints. Built-in generics such as list[str] and dict[str, int] have been valid since Python 3.9. X | None is the union with None. tuple[int, ...] means a tuple of ints of unknown length. TypedDict describes a dict with named keys.

A type checker is a separate program you run on purpose. mypy and Pyright both read annotations and report mismatches. They are third-party tools. Their answers can differ on hard cases. In a project, run the checker the same way you run tests, and treat a new error as a failed check. This browser runtime does not include either checker.

Group the library by the job, not by the alphabet. Text and formats: string methods, re, json, csv, textwrap. Numbers: math, statistics, random, decimal, fractions. Time: datetime, time, zoneinfo, calendar. Files and processes: pathlib, shutil, os, subprocess, tempfile. Data you keep: sqlite3, pickle with care, shelve rarely.

Most small tools are a file of records and a clock. json is for nested data and speaks Unicode. csv is for rows. Both need an encoding decision when they meet a file. datetime.date and datetime.datetime are aware of calendars. Attach a timezone when the clock time belongs to a place.
seeds.eg: import json from statistics import mean def average_score(payload): rows = json.loads(payload) return mean(row["score"] for row in rows)

seeds.ex: pathlib for names, subprocess to launch a program, sqlite3 to keep rows. Prefer Path over string surgery. subprocess.run takes a list of arguments when you want to avoid the shell. shell=True is a different, riskier mode. sqlite3 gives you a transactional file.

print is fine while you explore. logging is what you leave in a program. logging.getLogger(__name__) gives a logger named for the module. debug, info, warning, and error are levels, not moods. Configure the format once at the edge of the program. pdb.set_trace() stops a local process for inspection. It is not useful in this page.

A request names a method and a path. A response names a status and a body. GET reads. POST sends a body the server may store. Status 200 means the request was answered as success. 404 means the path is not there. 400 means the client sent something the server refuses to interpret. The body is bytes. JSON is a common way to put a dict in those bytes.

Flask is a WSGI microframework. You map a path to a function. Flask is maintained in the Pallets projects. An app is an instance, and a route is a function. WSGI is a synchronous convention between the app and a server. The development server is for your machine, not for the public internet.
seeds.eg: from flask import Flask app = Flask(__name__) @app.get("/health") def health(): return {"ok": True}

seeds.ex: FastAPI is an ASGI framework that uses type hints to describe parameters. FastAPI builds on Starlette and uses Pydantic to parse and document bodies. ASGI can run async routes. A def route runs in a threadpool. An async def route runs on the event loop, so it should not call blocking code directly. The automatic docs page is generated from the routes.
seeds.eg: from fastapi import FastAPI app = FastAPI() @app.get("/health") def health(): return {"ok": True}

seeds.ex: A list of dicts is a fine table until a library earns its import. csv.DictReader yields rows as dicts. You can filter them with a comprehension. This stays readable for thousands of rows. It gets clumsy for alignment, missing values, and grouped statistics. That is the moment to talk about pandas, not the first line of a homework file.

An ndarray stores one dense block of numbers and operates on all of them. NumPy is the array library underneath much of scientific Python. This site vendors NumPy 2.4.6. An array has a shape and a dtype. Arithmetic happens element by element. The mean of an array is a method. A Python loop over a million floats is the thing NumPy is designed to avoid.
seeds.eg: import numpy as np def mean_of(values): return float(np.asarray(values, dtype=float).mean())

seeds.ex: A DataFrame is a labeled table. This lab vendors pandas 3.0.2. A DataFrame has columns you can select by name. Boolean indexing filters rows. groupby splits rows by a key. pandas 2 made copy-on-write the direction of travel, and the 3.0 line continues that care about views and copies. Prefer returning a new frame to surprising inplace edits.
seeds.eg: import pandas as pd def column_sum(records, column): frame = pd.DataFrame(records) return int(frame[column].sum())

seeds.ex: Features, labels, training, and evaluation are ordinary ideas with sharp meanings. A feature is a measurement you decided to record. A label is the answer attached to an example. Training adjusts a model's parameters so its predictions move toward those labels on the training examples. Evaluation checks a set of examples the adjustment did not use.

y = w x + b is a model. Squared error is one way to judge it. Suppose you predict w times x plus b. The error is the prediction minus the actual y. For squared error, a small step subtracts a fraction of the error times x from w, and a fraction of the error from b. That is the whole idea of a linear model.
seeds.eg: def step(w, b, x, y, rate): error = (w * x + b) - y w = w - rate * error * x b = b - rate * error return w, b

seeds.ex: One library is for classical models. The other is for tensors and neural nets. scikit-learn fits and evaluates models such as linear models, trees, and clustering, with a fit and predict style. PyTorch is a tensor library used to build and train neural networks, with automatic differentiation.

An agent proposes a tool, you run it inside a limit, and you check the result. A practical loop has a task, a list of tools you wrote, a maximum number of steps, and a check that says whether the result is acceptable. The model can choose a bad tool or invent a fact. The tool should refuse work outside its job.

One command, one purpose, and a way to run it again. If you did it twice in a terminal, write it down as a script. Print a short summary of what changed. Return a non-zero exit status when the input is unusable, which in library code means raising, and at the edge means sys.exit. Keep the pure work in a function so a test can call it without the terminal.

Arguments, a folder, and rows are the usual ingredients. argparse turns sys.argv into values and writes the help text. The function that sums a column should not read sys.argv. It should take the rows. That split is what makes the exercise below possible in the browser, where you do not have the script's command line.
seeds.eg: def sum_column(rows, column): total = 0 for row in rows: total += int(row[column]) return total

seeds.ex: A script that deletes, emails, or fetches should show its work first. Print the files you would delete, and require an explicit flag before you delete them. Fetch only URLs you were asked to fetch, and respect the site's terms and a reasonable rate. Do not put credentials in the source file.

One project, one environment, so installs do not collide. python -m venv .venv is the standard-library way to create an environment. Activate it, then python -m pip install puts packages there. pip is the installer that ships with that workflow. uv is a third-party installer and resolver from Astral, written in Rust. Many people use it because it is fast.

The project file names the build system and, usually, the metadata. The packaging guide shows a pyproject.toml with a [build-system] table and a [project] table. The [project] fields are specified so different tools can read the name, version, and dependencies. A wheel is what you often install. An sdist is the source archive.

unittest or pytest for behavior. Ruff for style. Git for history. unittest is in the standard library. pytest is a third-party runner many projects prefer. Use one as the command you actually run. Ruff, also from Astral, lints and can format. Black is another third-party formatter. Neither is required by the language. Git is how you keep history.

Permissive licenses and the GPL answer different questions about sharing changes. The MIT license and the 3-clause BSD license are permissive. They ask you to keep the copyright notice. seeds.ti: How to read an exam page
seeds.ex: The exam code, the status, the passing score, and the price are the fields that change. Active means the institute is offering that version. Pending release and in development mean you should not tell a friend the new version is bookable. Discontinued means a previous version was retired.
General Python, data, and entry-level AI have public exam pages. PCPP2 does not have a finished syllabus. PCEP, Certified Entry-Level Python Programmer.

Language, then a finished project, then a specialty you can explain. First, write small programs until syntax, types, and functions feel ordinary. Then files, exceptions, modules, and tests, so a program can be run again. Then finish one project you can demo: a script, a small web route, or a table with a written check.

Explain a project, a cost, and a test. Skip memorized company secrets. Be ready to open a project and say what it does, which structure holds the data, what the slow operation would be, and which test would catch a mistake.

From a greeting to a file organizer. Each one names the skill it practices. Greeting. A function and a __main__ guard. You already have the shape from fundamentals. Guess. The game in this lab, rewritten as a Python script with a test for the higher/lower rule. CSV totals. Read a file with csv and sum a column.
